title: Pool Etiquette: 10 Unwritten Rules Every Player Should Know
description: New to the pool hall? Learn the 10 unwritten rules of pool etiquette, from staying still during a shot to shaking hands after a match, and play like a regular.
body:
You rack up, chalk your cue, and sink your first ball. Then someone at the next table gives you a friendly nod, and you realize you are about to break an unwritten rule you did not know existed. Don't worry. Pool etiquette is simple, mostly common sense, and knowing it makes every visit to the pool hall more fun for everyone.

With the Mosconi Cup in Orlando just two weeks away, you will see the world's best players follow many of these habits on TV. Here are the ten courtesies that make you look like a regular, even if it is your first night out.

1. Stay still when someone is shooting

This is the golden rule. When a player is down on a shot, avoid walking behind them, waving your cue around or making sudden noises. Pros at big events get a silent arena for a reason: a tiny distraction can ruin a shot. Wait until the ball stops rolling before you chat or move.

2. Don't stand in their line of sight

Players look down the table, not just at the cue ball. Find a spot to the side or behind your opponent, away from the line of the shot, and stay there until it is your turn.

3. Ask before you rack, and rack tight

Whoever lost the last game often racks, but it is polite to check what your opponent prefers. Take a moment to rack the balls tightly, with the right ball at the front for your game. A loose rack makes for a weak break and an annoyed opponent. If you need a refresher, our guides section has plenty of rules help.

4. Call your shots if the game needs it

In many games, such as 8-ball and 9-ball under some rule sets, you must name the ball and pocket in advance. Even in a casual game, saying it out loud avoids arguments later. Agree on the rules before the first break: are slop shots allowed, who breaks next, and what happens on a scratch?

5. Own your fouls

If you accidentally touch a ball with your sleeve or cue, say so right away. Honesty is the heart of pool. Players who call fouls on themselves earn respect fast, and it keeps the game fun rather than tense.

6. Be gentle with the table

Never sit on the rails, place drinks on the cloth or rest your cue tip against the felt. Use the bridge and the chalk as intended, and keep your chalk off the table surface. Tables are expensive, and a torn cloth ends the fun for everyone.

7. Chalk away from the table

Blue chalk dust on the felt affects how the balls roll. Step to the side to chalk your cue so that the dust does not land on the playing surface or on the balls.

8. Keep your cue to yourself

Other players' cues are personal gear. Don't pick one up without asking, and never lean on or tap someone else's cue. Likewise, keep your own cue in a case when you are not using it, so no one trips over it.

9. Respect the clock and the waiting list

At a busy hall, there may be a sign-up list or a "winner stays on" line for a table. Don't hog it for hours if others are waiting. If you are at a league night or tournament, watch the schedule so you are ready to play when your match is called. You can find upcoming events anytime on our tournament finder or calendar.

10. Win and lose with a smile

Shake hands after the match, say "good game," and thank your opponent. The pros do it at every major event, win or lose, and it is one of the best parts of the sport. If you got beaten, ask for a tip. Most players love to talk about the game.

Quick tips for your first night out

Arrive a little early so you can watch a few games and get a feel for the room. Ask the staff how table time works, whether it is by the hour or by the game. Bring your own cue if you have one, but house cues are perfectly fine for beginners. Most of all, relax: nearly everyone in a pool hall started out missing easy shots, and friendly players are usually happy to share advice with someone who asks politely.

Bonus: be a good spectator

Watching a match? Keep conversations quiet, silence your phone, and applaud after the shot is finished. Looking for something to do this weekend? Check what is happening this weekend and head out to watch some live pool.

The bottom line

Good etiquette is really just about respect: for your opponent, for the table, and for the game. Follow these ten habits and you will be welcome at any pool hall, from the corner bar to the biggest tournament stage. Which unwritten rule do you think matters most? Let us know on our Facebook Pages!
